newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Solana renews efforts to break expansion deadlock.
newsitem.headline: Solana renews efforts to break expansion deadlock.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana renewed attempts on Wednesday to try to find agreement within the alliance over which countries to invite to join the West's defence club at a special summit next month.

Solana has been charged with trying to end differences among NATO's 16 members over whether to limit membership to three former communist countries or extend it to five amid increasing signs the dispute could last to the eve of the summit in Madrid.

The United States, which has led the diplomatic push to take the new democracies into the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), said publicly last month it wanted to limit the first wave to Poland, Hungary and Czech Republic.

But France, with the backing of several other alliance states, wants Romania and Slovenia to be taken in at the same time -- arguing those countries have made sufficient progress and their inclusion would guarantee a wider European stability.

Solana has arranged a series of one-to-one meetings with alliance ambassadors over the next four days in the hope a consensus will emerge in time for a formal agreement by the policy-making North Atlantic Council next week.

NATO sources say, however, it is increasingly likely the issue will not now be finally resolved until shortly before the July 8-9 summit, intended to inaugurate a post-Cold War European security order.

"This one could well go down to the wire, so far there has been very little movement," said one official, noting nine countries, France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Canada, Turkey, Italy, Greece, Spain and Portugal, all supporting a broader expansion.

Leading western leaders attending last weekend's Group of Seven summit in Denver made no progress in overcoming the impasse with President Bill Clinton and President Jacques Chirac openly stating their preferences.

NATO sources say they believe the U.S. administration, with an eye on the right-wing Republican Congress which must ratify the enlargement, will not change its position, but may be pressured into some form of compromise deal.
"People are suggesting formulas whereby Romania and Slovenia are named as the next members," added the official.
NATO sources say much will depend on the final view of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl who has yet to come down on one side or the other.
"If Kohl goes for five, then the Americans will be under immense pressure to agree at least a face-saving formula for Chirac," said one diplomatic source.
Germany's Bundestag debates the issue on Friday and Solana has slated a meeting with Bonn's ambassador for Monday.

Several other countries, particularly the Nordic states, back the U.S. position, arguing too hasty an expansion would leave the alliance unwieldy, put back the time scale for a promised second wave, and involve unacceptably-high costs.
Denmark, Iceland and Norway have also said they would like to see parity of treatment between Romanian and the Balkan states -- Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia.
"Just because these countries were once in the Soviet Union does not mean they should be treated differently," Danish Defence Minister Hans Haekkerup recently told Reuters.
Alliance diplomats stress that NATO -- which operates by consensus -- is now committed to taking in at least three countries and to an "open door" policy thereafter.
"Essentially the leading three are 'in', and it is all now about finding a form of words for the others," said one envoy.
